3904.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mélans, from a derivation of Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“dark, black”). The feminine -αινα (-aina) originates from *-ih₂ via metathesis; see -ια (-ia).

3987.t: From φιλόσοφος (phĭlósophos, “lover of knowledge or wisdom”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā), from φίλος (phĭ́los, “beloved; loving”) + σοφός (sophós, “skilled with handcrafts; wise”).

3956.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ster- Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *str̥tós Proto-Hellenic *strətós Ancient Greek στρατός From Proto-Hellenic *strətós, from Proto-Indo-European *str̥tós, from *ster- (“to…

3902.t: From the root of μαίνομαι (maínomai, “to be mad or raving”), per J.B.

3983.t: From φάντασις (phắntăsĭs) + -ία (-ĭ́ā), from φαντάζω (phăntắzō, “to make visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine”).

3925.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂ Proto-Indo-European *périh₂ Proto-Hellenic *péřřa Ancient Greek πεῖρα From Proto-Hellenic *péřřa, from Proto-Indo-European *pér-ih₂ ~…

3949.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tseřřā́, from Proto-Indo-European *twer-yeh₂- (“seizing”), from *twerH- (“to grab, seize, enclose”).

3978.t: From Proto-Indo-European *trep- (“to turn”); cognate with Latin trepit (“turns”, verb), Sanskrit त्रपते (trápate, “feels ashamed, becomes timid or perplexed”), and Hittite 𒋼𒊑𒅁𒍣 (te-ri-ip-zi /⁠teripzi⁠/, “to plough”).

3946.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pít͏̌t͏̌a, from Proto-Indo-European *pik- (“pitch, resin”). Cognate with Latin pix, Proto-Slavic *pьkъlъ.

3909.t: Of uncertain origin, though likely inherited (as opposed to borrowed from a substrate).

3998.t: From χείμερος (kheímeros, “wintry, stormy”) + -ινός (-inós), or directly from Proto-Indo-European [Term?] and cognate with Latin hībernus.

3906.t: From μυριάς (mūriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (mūríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”).

3996.t: According to Beekes, of unknown or Pre-Greek origin, and unrelated to Armenian խաղ (xaġ, “game, pastime”) (a connection would require a Proto-Indo-European *kʰ, which is unheard of for inherited words).

3940.t: Apparently from προσ- (pros-, “pro-”) + φατός (phatós, “slain”), thus originally a hunting or fishing term meaning "lately or freshly slain", with semantic broadening being facilitated once the second element's origin had become opaque to Greek speakers.

3990.t: From φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry; to bring, fetch”) + -έω (-éō, frequentative verbal suffix); from Proto-Hellenic *pʰoréyō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoréyeti. Cognate with Sanskrit भारयति (bhāráyati).

3907.t: Some have tried a connection with Old Armenian ներկ (nerk, “color”), deriving both from a Proto-Indo-European root *(s)negʷro-, because often the deer and the hind are called after their variegated color (compare πρόξ (próx, “roe deer”) and περκνός…

3944.t: Perhaps a loanword from Thracian considering the origin of this type of shield. Usually connected with Latin pellis (“skin”) and Ancient Greek πέλμα (pélma, “sole of the foot”), so from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover”).

3927.t: From Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to approach”). By surface analysis, an adjectival formation from πέλας (pélas, “near, nearby”).

3981.t: From Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“to bear”), like τελαμών (telamṓn, “strap, belt”) and τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance, scale”).

3939.t: Etymology tree Ancient Greek πρίω (príō) Proto-Indo-European *-ō Ancient Greek -ων (-ōn) Ancient Greek πρίων From πρίω (príō, “to saw, to cut”) + -ων (-ōn).

3929.t: From πορφύρα (porphúrā) + -εος (-eos), of unknown, perhaps Semitic, origin. The association with πορφύρω (porphúrō, “to surge up (of waves)”), through an association with the “wine-dark sea”, is a folk etymology.

3945.t: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)penh₁- (“to weave, spin”), with semantic shift "to weave, stretch" > "to tense, strain" > "to exert oneself".

3960.t: From συν- (sun-, “with, together”) + χωρέω (khōréō, “to withdraw, give way”).

3984.t: From φέρω (phérō, “bring”) + -νή (-nḗ, “a suffix added to verbal stems or adjectives to form feminine nouns.”) The nasal-suffix is also present in Old Armenian բեռն (beṙn) and Lithuanian bernas.

3991.t: From the verb φρίσσω (phríssō, “to shiver, shudder, tremble”).

3975.t: From a reduplicated form of Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- + -αίνω (-aínō).
